angle: AI can't brainstorm from nothing. Humans bring the first 2-3 ideas and Claude gets you to 10
post_first_line: 2 or 3 ideas. That's all Claude needs.
linkedin_post:
2 or 3 ideas. That's all Claude needs.

But without them, it has nothing to build on.

A couple weeks ago, Sarah came by our office and we ran a brainstorming session on how we could be betting more broadly as a team.

We went through the business, covering all the channels we run today, where we're seeing success, and where we're not. We left with a bunch of ideas on how to improve what we're doing.

AI can amplify a session like that. But the kernels of insight still need to come from people.

The first 2 or 3 ideas are what help Claude get you to ideas 7 through 10.

AI doesn't brainstorm from nothing. It multiplies what you bring to it.

So if your Claude brainstorms feel generic, look at what you fed it first.

Where do your best starting ideas come from?

Slide 2: Sarah and I ran a brainstorm on betting more broadly.
Slide 3: We reviewed every channel: what works, what doesn't.
Slide 4: AI can amplify a session like that.
Slide 5: But the kernels of insight still come from people.
Slide 6: Your first 2 or 3 ideas are the seed.
Slide 7: Those seeds help Claude get you to ideas 7 through 10.
Slide 8: Bring the seeds. Let AI do the multiplying.

lesson.title: Humans Seed, AI Multiplies
takeaways: AI amplifies brainstorming but doesn't replace the original insight from people.
The first 2 or 3 ideas are what help Claude reach ideas 7 through 10.
Reviewing what's working and what isn't gives you the raw material for good seeds.
lesson.exercise: Before opening Claude, write down 2 or 3 ideas of your own on one channel you run. Then give them to Claude and ask it to extend the list to 10.

angle: Feeling behind on AI? Start with small chats, then build your first skill
post_first_line: Everyone feels behind on AI right now.
linkedin_post:
Everyone feels behind on AI right now.

I think the anxiety comes from one specific mistake.

We've been going through our own journey internally, using these products over the past few months. The anxiety is real. People keep asking what they should be doing and how it's all supposed to work.

My advice: start with small things.

Don't force yourself into some crazy complicated use case.

Run a few chats in Claude. Then move into building your first skill.

It doesn't need to be perfect.

The intuition comes from trying things, not from reading about them as a third party.

What's the first thing you tried in Claude?

lesson.title: Feeling behind on AI? Start small and build from there
takeaways: Anxiety about AI is common, and it's usually triggered by trying to start with something too complicated.
A simple path works: run chats in Claude first, then build your first skill.
Intuition is built by trying things yourself, not by reading about them as a third party.
lesson.exercise: Open Claude today and run three small chats on real work you're already doing. Then pick one repeatable task and turn it into your first skill, even if it's imperfect.

angle: Build the lead magnet, not a beautiful page: always include a CTA
post_first_line: Under 30 seconds to build a landing page.
linkedin_post:
Under 30 seconds to build a landing page.

The page itself wasn't the interesting part. What Sarah Charlton put on it was.

Sarah Charlton built a concept page with a talk to sales button, a hero image, and a toggle designed to make the experience more fun. It also had inputs a teammate named Quentin asked for, a headline with detail, and some customer quotes.

At the end, the page emails results to visitors and shows a second CTA.

Sarah Charlton's rule: you're doing this to build a lead magnet, not a beautiful page.

That's why a CTA is always on it. Looking at the page, you wouldn't guess it took under 30 seconds to build.

When a page takes seconds to make, polish stops being the goal. Conversion is.

What's the first CTA you'd put on a lead magnet?
carousel: Slide 1: This landing page took under 30 seconds to build.
Slide 2: Sarah Charlton's rule: build a lead magnet, not a beautiful page.
Slide 3: Always include a CTA. Always.
Slide 4: Start with a hero image and a headline with detail.
Slide 5: Add a fun toggle and the inputs your team asked for.
Slide 6: Drop in customer quotes to build trust.
Slide 7: End by emailing results to visitors, with a second CTA.
Slide 8: When pages build in seconds, conversion beats polish.

lesson.title: Build the lead magnet, not a beautiful page
takeaways: A lead magnet exists to convert, so every page needs a CTA.
Include a hero image, headline with detail, customer quotes, and inputs your team wants.
Close the page with emailed results and a second CTA.
lesson.exercise: Sketch a one-page concept for your next lead magnet: list the hero, headline, customer quotes, and two CTAs (one at the top, one after results are emailed). Then build a rough version fast.

caption: Lead magnet, not beauty

angle: We've never posted a LinkedIn post straight out of AI, and here's why
linkedin_post:
Zero AI-written posts. Ever.

I've written on LinkedIn for the past couple years, and there's a reason I never publish what AI gives me.

Not once have we taken a post straight out of AI and put it up. It's just not good enough.

It's not interesting. It doesn't have the taste or care that someone good at marketing brings.

It also doesn't understand what's happening in the zeitgeist right now, or how people are feeling about things.

And I'm not confident it's going to take a lot to close that gap, but today it's still there.

So this is one area where I personally get no leverage out of it.

Where do you draw the line with AI in your content?

Slide 2: I've written on LinkedIn for a couple of years.

Slide 8: For now, writing is where I get no AI leverage.

lesson.title: Why AI drafts don't make it to the feed
takeaways: AI output lacks the taste and care a good marketer brings.
It doesn't understand the zeitgeist or how people feel about things right now.
Interesting is the bar, and raw AI drafts don't clear it.
lesson.exercise: Take your last AI-generated draft and mark every line that shows no awareness of what your audience is feeling this week. Rewrite those lines yourself before publishing.

angle: Don't ask AI to invent your ROI math. Bring the logic, let it build the page
linkedin_post:
12 pages of size 12 font.

That was the ROI calculator instructions Sarah Charlton started with.

Sarah Charlton's point: you don't tell AI to figure out the ROI on Unify. That isn't something you can delegate, and you don't want AI running that logic for you.

The logic has to come from a person. In this case, Quentin built the calculator and a diagram to go with it.

The 12-page version was too much for a 15-minute session. So Sarah Charlton asked Claude to turn it into something much simpler that could be built in the time available.

Claude came back with a really simple calculator. That simplified Unify ROI calculator is what got used for the session.

The split is clear: people own the math, AI handles the build and the simplification.

Where do you draw the line with AI?
carousel: Slide 1: Don't ask AI to invent your ROI math.
Slide 2: Sarah Charlton started with 12 pages of detailed instructions.
Slide 3: ROI logic isn't something you can delegate to AI.
Slide 4: Quentin built the calculator and the diagram first.
Slide 5: Then Claude was asked to simplify it for 15 minutes.
Slide 6: The result: a really simple calculator, built for the session.
Slide 7: You own the logic. AI helps build the page.

lesson.title: Bring the logic, let AI build the page
takeaways: ROI math is not something to delegate to AI. The reasoning has to come from you.
A detailed human-built framework is the right starting input, even if it's too long to use as is.
AI is useful for simplifying that framework into something buildable in the time you have.
lesson.exercise: Write down the logic behind one calculation you rely on, such as ROI. Then ask AI to turn it into a simpler version you could build in 15 minutes.

caption: Don't delegate your ROI math

angle: Sales isn't AI vs. human anymore. AI is table stakes and selling stays human-to-human
post_first_line: Sales is now a human plus AI story.
linkedin_post:
Sales is now a human plus AI story.

The "AI will replace sales" narrative from a year or two ago didn't hold up.

Sarah Charlton framed the shift this way: AI should absorb the research and administration work. Selling itself is inherently a human-to-human thing, and that's not going anywhere.

The more interesting question is how the best sellers are thinking about using AI to get leverage.

AI is now table stakes. It's a sales plus AI use case, not a sales versus AI debate.

Which part of your sales work should AI absorb first?

Slide 2: The "AI will replace sales" narrative didn't hold up.
Slide 3: AI should absorb research and administration work.

lesson.title: Sales Is Human Plus AI
takeaways: The AI-replaces-sales story has been replaced by a sales plus AI story.
AI should absorb research and administration so sellers can focus on selling.
Selling is inherently human-to-human, while AI use is now table stakes.
lesson.exercise: List your team's weekly tasks and mark which are research or administration. Pick one to hand to AI this week, and note what time you reinvest in conversations with buyers.
